title: SCT Temporal Change Detection — Final Comprehensive Report
objective: Measure scalloped terrain scarp retreat rates from HiRISE temporal image pairs using sub-pixel phase correlation

executive_summary.verdict: UNABLE TO CONFIRM REAL SCARP RETREAT
executive_summary.summary: While Phase 1-2 demonstrated a sound methodology with strong statistical signal on a single pair, Phase 3B cross-validation with independent classification revealed that the signal does NOT replicate across pairs. The critical Pair 0 vs Pair 1 diagnostic shows that two images of the SAME terrain with nearly identical temporal baselines produce opposite results (excess=+0.84m vs -0.02m). Spatial autocorrelation analysis confirms the detected signal is spatially smooth (r>0.99), consistent with systematic co-registration or illumination artifact rather than localized terrain change.
key_findings: Phase 1: Pipeline methodology validated — 42% recovery rate, zero false positives on null injection
Phase 2: Strong statistical signal on Pair 0 (p=5e-16), but based on a single pair
Phase 3B: Cross-validation with independent classification — 3/6 pairs show significant excess, but R²=0.009 (NO proportionality with temporal baseline), CV=2.15 (wildly inconsistent rates)
Diagnostic: Pair 0 vs Pair 1 cover 96.6% of the same ground yet give opposite results — the 0.84m excess in Pair 0 is not reproducible
Diagnostic: Displacement in Pair 0 has 0.999 spatial autocorrelation — consistent with systematic artifact, not localized scarp retreat

pipeline: 1. HiRISE RDR (RED channel) JP2 images at 0.25 m/px native resolution
2. Spatial co-registration via projected CRS overlap extraction + FFT bulk alignment
3. Sub-pixel phase correlation (chip=256px, step=128px, upsample=100x → 2.5mm precision)
4. Order-3 polynomial detrending to remove spatially-varying registration residuals
5. Terrain classification: MarsLandformNet (Pair 0) or gradient-percentile (other pairs)
6. Statistical comparison: Mann-Whitney U test (scarp vs stable displacement distributions)
methodology.calibration: Phase 1 synthetic injection test established 42% recovery rate → ×2.38 correction factor
methodology.quality_filters: SNR > 3.0 for chip validity; NCC > 0.5 for Phase 2 high-confidence subset

phase_1_synthetic_validation.purpose: Validate pipeline methodology and determine calibration factor
phase_1_synthetic_validation.method: Inject known sub-pixel displacements (0.1–1.0 px) into real HiRISE imagery and measure recovery
phase_1_synthetic_validation.conclusion: Pipeline methodology is sound. Consistent ~42% attenuation is a systematic bias correctable by ×2.38 calibration.

phase_2_polynomial_detrending.purpose: Remove spatially-varying co-registration residuals to improve signal-to-noise
phase_2_polynomial_detrending.conclusion: Order-3 polynomial detrending reduces stable noise 3.4× and improves significance by 11 orders of magnitude. Clear excess displacement in scarp terrain detected with very high confidence. However, cross-validation (Phase 3B) later revealed this signal does not replicate.

phase_3_multi_pair_batch.purpose: Process all 10 ranked temporal pairs to corroborate single-pair measurement
phase_3_multi_pair_batch.approach: Two-pass: (1) raw correlation for data-driven classification, (2) detrended correlation with cleaned stable reference. Pair 0 uses MarsLandformNet classification.

classification_bias_analysis.issue: The two-pass approach selects high-displacement chips as 'scarp' by definition, creating circular reasoning that guarantees positive excess regardless of actual terrain change.
classification_bias_analysis.evidence: Retreat rates span 120× range (0.10–12.5 m/My); rates inversely correlate with temporal baseline (r=-0.53), consistent with a fixed classification artifact rather than real signal.
classification_bias_analysis.conclusion: Only Pair 0 (MarsLandformNet classification) provides an unbiased measurement. Other pairs demonstrate the pipeline runs but their retreat rates are inflated by selection bias.

phase_3b_cross_validation.purpose: Re-analyze all pairs with displacement-INDEPENDENT classification to eliminate circular bias

classification_methods.pair_1: MarsLandformNet mapped via shared base image (PSP_007173_2245)
classification_methods.others: Gradient-percentile (top 40% by image gradient → scarp, bottom 25% → stable)

proportionality_test.description: If real retreat, excess should scale linearly with temporal baseline
proportionality_test.verdict: DOES NOT SUPPORT real retreat — no proportionality (R²≈0), wildly inconsistent rates (CV>2)

phase_4_diagnostic.purpose: Investigate WHY Pair 0 and Pair 1 give opposite results despite covering the same terrain

diagnostic_1_overlap_geometry.finding: Center-crops overlap 96.6% — they analyze effectively the same ground
diagnostic_1_overlap_geometry.conclusion: The discrepancy is NOT due to different terrain patches. Pair 0 and Pair 1 see the same scallops.

diagnostic_2_illumination.finding: Pair 0 has SMALLER illumination difference than Pair 1, yet shows STRONG signal while Pair 1 shows none. This is inconsistent with both real retreat (both should show it) AND illumination artifact (Pair 1 should show more).

excess_direction_vs_illumination.pair_0: Excess vector direction 27.3° vs illumination direction 218.4° (Δ=168.9° — nearly opposite)
excess_direction_vs_illumination.pair_1: Excess vector direction 249.9° vs illumination direction 113.8° (Δ=136.1°)

diagnostic_2_illumination.conclusion: No consistent correlation between excess displacement direction and illumination difference direction across pairs. Illumination artifact alone does not explain the pattern.

diagnostic_3_spatial_autocorrelation.finding: Both pairs show very high spatial autocorrelation (r>0.95), meaning displacement varies SMOOTHLY across the image. This is characteristic of systematic registration residuals, not localized scarp retreat.

pair_0_displacement_stats.note: Pair 0 has large systematic eastward drift (+2.7m mean column displacement) that polynomial detrending partially removes

pair_1_displacement_stats.note: Pair 1 has much smaller, more uniform displacement — better aligned

diagnostic_3_spatial_autocorrelation.conclusion: Pair 0's 'excess' may be residual systematic drift that happens to correlate with scarp locations because both scarps and drift are spatially structured. Pair 1's better alignment eliminates this residual, revealing no real signal.

phase_4_diagnostic.overall_diagnostic_conclusion: The 0.84m excess in Pair 0 is most likely a spatially-structured co-registration residual rather than real terrain retreat. Evidence: (1) not reproducible in Pair 1 with same terrain, (2) spatially smooth (r=0.999) rather than localized, (3) large systematic drift component (+2.7m column mean), (4) no proportionality with temporal baseline across pairs.

final_assessment.verdict: UNABLE TO CONFIRM REAL SCARP RETREAT
final_assessment.confidence: HIGH that the measured signal is artifact, not real retreat
reasoning: The pipeline methodology is validated (Phase 1) and produces statistically significant results on individual pairs (Phase 2)
However, the signal does NOT replicate: Pair 0 and Pair 1 cover the same terrain but give opposite results
The detected displacement is spatially smooth (lag-1 autocorrelation r=0.999), inconsistent with localized scarp retreat
No proportionality between excess displacement and temporal baseline (R²=0.009)
Pair 0 has large systematic drift (+2.7m mean column displacement) suggesting incomplete co-registration correction

The excess likely arises because scarp terrain has different geometric/topographic properties that interact differently with registration residuals (parallax, slope-dependent geocoding error, shadow-dependent correlation behavior)
what_would_be_needed: Independent confirmation from a DIFFERENT method (e.g., manual scarp edge digitization, shadow length measurement)
Running MarsLandformNet on ALL pairs for consistent independent classification
Sub-meter resolution DEM differencing (stereo-derived DEMs from different epochs)
Improved co-registration using feature-based methods (SIFT/ORB on stable features) rather than FFT bulk alignment
Analysis of the FULL overlap region, not just 4.3% center-crop

retreat_rate_upper_bound.note: Given that the signal appears to be artifact, we can estimate an upper bound on retreat rate from the noise floor
retreat_rate_upper_bound.interpretation: If scarp retreat exists at this location, it is below ~33 cm/Mars-yr (2σ detection limit) given current methodology

limitations: Single location with independent (MarsLandformNet) classification — multi-site analysis requires model inference capability
42% recovery rate means true displacement may be larger; calibration factor has uncertainty
Co-registration accuracy is insufficient to separate real sub-pixel terrain change from registration residuals
Center-crop to 8192×8192 px means only ~4.3% of full overlap is analyzed
Gradient-based terrain classification is a poor proxy for actual landform classification
3 of 10 pairs failed due to truncated JP2 downloads
No GPU available for MarsLandformNet inference on additional pairs
Phase correlation is inherently sensitive to any systematic difference between images (illumination, atmospheric, sensor)
positive_outcomes: Validated sub-pixel phase correlation pipeline for Mars surface change detection
Demonstrated synthetic injection testing as a rigorous calibration methodology
Identified critical failure mode (classification circularity) in displacement-based landform classification
Produced a multi-pair processing framework that can be reused with improved classification
Established that scarp retreat at this location, if present, is below ~33 cm/Mars-yr
The pipeline and diagnostic framework are ready for application to sites with stronger expected signal
